full_judgment:
6. Mr. Khan next contends that the learned Munsif was correct in holding that She suit was bad for defect of parties. The instant suit is against defendants allegedly dispossessed the plaintiff on 7.12.66. The alleged act of dispossession is an independent act giving rise to the cause of action for the instant suit. The persons who dispossessed the plaintiff are the only necessary parties in a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act for recovery of khas possession. The contention that the plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 83 of 1966 on 24-5-66 against certain officers of the erstwhile Government of East Pakistan and as such, these impleaded in Title Suit No. 83 of 1966 are necessary parties in the suit appears to be misconceived. The cause of action for the said Title Suit No. 83 of 1966 was completely different and had no connection whatsoever with the subsequent suit filed on 10.5.67 under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act. It could not be pointed out by Mr. Khan that in the facts and circumstances of the instant case, these officers of the erstwhile Province of East Pakistan are necessary parties to the present action. In that suit the instant defendants were not impleaded since there was no overt act by these defendants when the cause for that suit arose. Mr. Khan has further urged that the defendants entered into possession of the suit land days before the alleged date of dispossession on the assurance of some officers of the then Government. There is no material on record to support this contention. In the written statement filed by the defendants, it has been stated that the application of the defendants for settlement was under investigation. It has been clearly stated that the defendant No. 1 entered into possession of the suit properties on 8.12.66. In the affidavit in opposition before this court it has been stated that" this deponent filed applications before the Sub-Divisional Officer, Moulvi Bazar on 30.11.66 stating that the suit homestead is lying vacant and the same may be settled with this deponent. That on receipt of this application, the Sub-divisional Officer, Moulvi Bazar asked this deponent to occupy that house provisionally pending final allotment by the authorities to whom his application has already been forwarded and as such on 7.12.66 the petitioners' family entered into the house and has been staying thereafter reconstructing the house." Thus from the written statement as also the affidavit-in-opposition, it appears that before 7.12.66 the defendants were not in possession of the disputed property which is a homestead and a tank. Mr. Khan has also drawn the attention of the court to Exhibit E, a Memo granted by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) dated 192-68 granting settlement in favour of Shamsur Rahman from 1-1-67 to 31.12.67. This appears to be the basis of defendants entry into the suit land. This document conclusively indicates that before 19.2.68 the day on which it was issued, Shamsur Rahman was not authorised in law to enter into possession of the properties in suit. In the circumstances the finding of the learned Munsif that the defendant entered into the suit land illegally and by dispossession is proved by Ext. E the basis document of the contesting defendants. There is nothing on record to indicate that on or before 7.12.66 the suit property was in possession of the custodian as Enemy Property and that the defendants acquired lawful authority to enter into the same.  8. The materials on record disclose that the plaintiff's possession as a co-sharer was not disputed. There is no evidence to indicate that the plaintiff was dispossessed by the defendants. The learned Munsif has found on consideration of evidence that the defendants "entered into the suit land illegally and by dispossession,." There is no dispute that the suit is in time, as observed earlier, the defendants of Title Suit No, 83 of 1966 are not necessary parties in the instant suit. The learned Munsif refused a decree in favour of the plaintiff because of "legal difficulties." According to the learned Munsif the "legal difficulties" were (1) plaintiff has got no locus standi to file the suit because his very foundation of claim has been removed." and (2) "the parties of T. S. No. 83 of 1966 are necessary in this suit, So, the suit is bad for defect of parties" Mr. T.H. Khan did not challenge that the plaintiff is a co-sharer in the suit land because of the obvious reason that there was no materials before the trial court indicating that the plaintiff was not a co-sharer in possession of the suit land. The trial court did not also characterise him as such. According to the learned Munsif, the power of attorney became invalid due to Ordinance I of 1964 and as such the plaintiff had to locus standi to file the suit. In fact of the instant case, Ordinance I of 1964 has no role to play since the plaintiff is a cc-sharer in possession of the suit land. The part attributed to Ordinance I of 1964 by the learned Munsif is apparently misconceived. Ordinance I of 1964 being a post Constitutional law was violative of fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution and was dead for all purposes. Reference way profitably be made to the case of Abdul Majid Bepari Vs Kashem Ali Maloo XXVII Dacca Law Reports 1 (High Court Division,) where East Pakistan Ordinance I of 1964 (E. P. Disturbed Persons (Rehabilitation) Ordinance, has been found to be dead for all purposes and void abinitin. In the circumstances, it does not appear that there is any legal bar for the plaintiff in getting a decree for recovery of khas possession after evicting the defendants from the suit land.
